headline: High: TREK’s collaborative browser/MCP stack can ingest and act on content from a broad-egress content source, creating prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-action risk.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: TREK explicitly uses browsers and MCP, and its real-time collaborative model can ingest external content; awesome-cli-apps is a content-writing/listing source with broad network egress. That creates a plausible instruction-injection bridge if TREK consumes content from A or copied outputs, though no direct shared channel is documented. Uncertainty keeps this at medium rather than low.
conditions: IF TREK ingests content from awesome-cli-apps or its rendered pages as instructions, injection is possible.
IF a shared MCP server or clipboard bridge is introduced, attacker-controlled text can cross from A to B.
mitigations: Disable automatic instruction-following on imported text.
Require provenance labels for all external content before B parses it.
Restrict MCP tools to allowlisted domains and schemas.
Use a manual review step for any content copied from A into B.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and provenance tracking.

B_data_leakage.rationale: B touches sensitive travel data, reservations, email addresses, API keys, and MFA secrets, and it has files plus networked APIs. A is a broad-egress content source, so if B forwards imported content or logs to external services, leakage can occur. A itself does not show sensitive-data handling, so the main exposure is B’s default surface, not a proven cross-agent exfiltration path.
conditions: IF B stores or forwards imported content from A into logs, uploads, or API calls, sensitive data can leak.
IF A is used to generate or transform travel documents that B then uploads, those contents may leave the local workspace.
mitigations: Avoid placing secrets in any content passed from A to B.
Turn off verbose logging for B during shared workflows.
Review uploads/ and trek.log for accidental sensitive content.
Limit B’s outbound API calls to necessary destinations only.
requires-engineering: separate secret-bearing data from collaborative content.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A has broad network egress, while B has allowlisted egress, browser control, MCP, and collaborative real-time sessions with multiple instances. Even without explicit filesystem write claims, overlapping mutable surfaces and concurrent sessions create coordination risk if both agents act on the same resources or MCP endpoints. Because write isolation is not documented, uncertainty escalates to medium.
conditions: IF both agents target the same MCP server or shared backend, conflicting writes can occur.
IF A and B are run concurrently against the same travel workspace, race conditions may overwrite state.
mitigations: Assign separate workspaces per agent.
Serialize writes through one operator-controlled queue.
Disable concurrent instances during shared edits.
Restrict B’s MCP access to read-only where possible.
requires-engineering: add locking around shared mutable resources.

D_cascading_error.rationale: B is a real-time collaborative travel planner with AI built in, browsers, and MCP, so it can plausibly treat upstream content as actionable. A is a content-writing/listing source with broad egress, meaning its outputs could be imported into B and then rendered or acted on without verification. That creates a default-dangerous cascade from content to downstream actions.
conditions: IF B uses A-generated text as itinerary facts or booking instructions without verification, downstream errors can propagate.
IF B auto-executes actions from imported content, a single bad item from A can affect multiple reservations or documents.
mitigations: Require human verification before B acts on imported content.
Mark A-derived content as untrusted in B.
Disable auto-booking or auto-send for imported items.
Cross-check critical facts against primary sources.
requires-engineering: add validation gates before downstream actions.

E_compliance.rationale: B explicitly handles reservations, documents, photos, country visit history, user accounts, email addresses, confirmation numbers, API keys, and MFA secrets, and it is self-hosted with OIDC/MCP integrations. A is only a content-writing/listing source, so the compliance concern is B’s handling of regulated or sensitive travel data; if A is used to process or display that data, the pair can breach retention or residency expectations. No stronger mitigation is documented.
conditions: IF EU PII or travel documents are routed through B without a DPA or residency controls, compliance risk is high.
IF B logs or retains secrets from shared content, retention and access controls may be violated.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of A-generated content.
Review B’s retention settings and logs today.
Limit access to secrets in B to named operators only.
Confirm residency and DPA coverage for external APIs.
requires-engineering: implement data-class-specific retention and residency controls.
